title: The Story of Tea
topic: The history and trade of tea
context:
Tea is the most widely consumed beverage in the world after water, yet its origins lie in a single plant, Camellia sinensis, native to the forests of south-west China. According to legend, the emperor Shennong discovered the drink around 2737 BC when leaves from a wild tree blew into his boiling water, but archaeologists have found evidence of tea drinking only from about the second century BC. Early on, tea was valued as a medicine rather than a pleasure, and it was often boiled with onions, ginger and orange peel.

By the Tang dynasty, tea had become a fashionable drink among scholars and monks. Monks drank it to stay awake during long hours of meditation, and Buddhist travellers carried seeds to Japan in the ninth century. Tea was compressed into hard bricks for transport, and these bricks even served as currency along the trade routes of Central Asia. Under the Song dynasty, fine powdered tea was whisked in bowls, a custom that later inspired the Japanese tea ceremony.

Europeans encountered tea in the sixteenth century, when Portuguese traders brought small quantities home. It was the Dutch who first imported it on a large scale, and from there it reached Britain, where Catherine of Braganza, the wife of Charles II, helped popularise it at court. For a long time tea was so expensive that it was kept under lock and key, and smuggling flourished, since high taxes made legal tea cost far more than it should. By 1800, the British were buying so much that the East India Company needed a way to pay for it without draining its silver reserves. Meanwhile, a new social habit grew up at home: the custom of afternoon tea emerged in the 1840s, when a duchess began asking for light refreshments to fill the long gap before dinner.

The solution was a trade in opium grown in India and sold illegally in China, which led to the Opium Wars of the nineteenth century. At the same time the company sought to break China's monopoly on tea by growing the plant elsewhere. In 1848, the botanist Robert Fortune smuggled seedlings and workers out of China, and plantations were soon established in Assam and Darjeeling. Within a few decades, India and later Sri Lanka had overtaken China as major exporters.

Today the industry employs millions of workers, many of them women who pick the leaves by hand, since machines damage the delicate shoots. Wages on some plantations remain low, and campaigners have pressed companies to adopt certification schemes. Climate change is a further concern, as warmer temperatures and irregular rain are altering the flavour and yield of tea grown at high altitude. Researchers are experimenting with heat-tolerant varieties to protect the crop, although it will take years to know whether they match the taste of traditional bushes.
